transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-27
Start: 14:30 UTC
Duration: 54 minutes
Location: Zoom call (recorded)
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Leo (Redwood SE), Dr. Priya Narang (CTO), Alex Mercer (Lead DevOps), Sandra Liu (CISO)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be incomplete):
Nova Clinic evaluating Redwood Private on-prem airgapped option for clinical inference. Primary concerns: update/patch process for airgapped nodes, hardware/driver compatibility, KMS/HSM integration for keys, SOC2/ISO artifacts, fallback options in case of failure, maintenance windows, and throughput/latency targets for inference. Next steps include sharing deployment checklist, scheduling hardware sizing, and providing inventory.

Topics detected: onboarding, airgapped updates, hardware sizing, compliance, rollback/fallback, model pinning, KV cache, latency targets.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I think we can get started. Um, hi Priya, Alex, Sandra, really appreciate you taking the time.

[00:12] Dr. Priya: Thanks, Maya. Yep, good to meet you both, um, short intro — we're looking to replace a pilot we're running with a more regulated-friendly setup, so on-prem, sealed environment is top of mind.

[00:25] Maya: Totally. Quick intro from our side — I'm Maya Patel, AE — and Leo is our SE focused on private deployments and on-prem runtimes. We'll mainly be listening to your constraints and try to map the right option — hosted, dedicated, or private.

[00:39] Leo: Hi folks. I'm Leo. I do a lot of the compatibility and sizing work and usually dive into hardware, drivers, and the update flows.

[00:47] Alex: Hey. We run most of our workloads on DGX-class boxes — a mix, some H100s, a few A100s. All on isolated VLANs, no internet from the ML cluster side.

[00:58] Sandra: From security, we're primarily concerned with key management and ensuring auditability — KMS or HSM integration, immutable logs, SSO with SAML, RBAC, and of course SOC 2 artifacts.

[01:10] Maya: Great. That matches what we've seen — everyone in regulated health wants that stack. A couple of high-level questions before we get into the weeds: what's your target latency and throughput? And who will own patching and updates?

[01:23] Dr. Priya: Latency needs to be sub-200ms p99 for some front-line clinical decisions, for others we can tolerate up to 700ms. Throughput starts small — 50 qps burst to 100 qps expected in six months. Patching, ideally the customer's side, but we'd like a secure, Redwood-provided update artifact and verification process.

[01:40] Leo: Understood. For an airgapped deployment we provide signed update bundles — basically binary artifacts packaged with checksums and signatures. Customers transfer via secure medium. We also provide an offline installer and a verification tool that validates signatures against a public key.

[01:55] Alex: By secure medium, you mean like sneakernet — USB or something? Firmware and security teams will need details. Also curious about whether the runtime requires outbound calls for licensing checks.

[02:06] Leo: No runtime outbound calls required — for Private deployments, everything can be configured to run without outbound. We do optionally offer an on-prem control plane that talks to Redwood's control plane via proxy if customers want telemetry — but that's opt-in and can be disabled.

[02:18] Sandra: How about KMS? We use an on-prem HSM and have strict key rotation policies. Can Redwood integrate with customer KMS/HSM or do we have to provide keys in files?

[02:28] Maya: Short answer: we can integrate with customer KMS/HSM. We have documented KMS integration patterns — Leo can walk through the auth modes and key wrapping approaches.

[02:36] Leo: Right — our private package supports either: 1) customer-managed KMS/HSM via PKCS#11 or KMIP, or 2) a sealed key approach where an operator loads a wrapped key into the node. For auditability we log key operations to an append-only audit store (local) and optionally forward to your SIEM if you enable a telemetry proxy.

[02:53] Dr. Priya: Sounds good. On the hardware side, we're worried about GPU drivers and kernel compatibility — we have mixed OS images in the cluster. We don't have a single golden image yet.

[03:05] Leo: Mixed images are okay but complicate the compatibility matrix. For example, certain optimized kernels for H100 require CUDA 12.x and specific driver versions. If you're mixing A100 and H100, we'll need to either partition pools or ensure the runtime builds for the lowest common denominator.

[03:21] Alex: We're fine partitioning, but want to avoid large perf regressions. Also, how big is the redis/kv cache footprint? We do not want NVMe saturation.

[03:32] Leo: The KV cache is in-memory by default but we support spill-to-disk (NVMe) for very large prefix caches. We usually recommend NVMe for high concurrency but for your qps numbers you can likely fit most working sets in memory on 512GB nodes; we'll run a sizing exercise.

[03:47] Maya: Quick Q, Priya — what's the timeframe for pilot vs production?

[03:52] Dr. Priya: We want a pilot in 6 weeks, production in 3 months if pilot goes well.

[03:58] Maya: Ok that's tight but doable. We'll propose a minimum viable pilot plan.

[04:05] Alex: One question on model lifecycle: can we pin model versions and do rollbacks without network access?

[04:11] Leo: Yes — model artifacts are stored locally; rollouts are orchestrated by an on-prem controller. You can pin versions and roll back. The controller accepts signed manifests that instruct the node to fetch the model from local artefact stores; if you're fully sealed, you distribute artifacts via secure media.

[04:27] Dr. Priya: Good. What about fallback to hosted Redwood if our cluster is degraded? We are concerned about PII leaving the premises — can't do that for some workloads.

[04:36] Maya: We recommend a policy model: sensitive routes marked 'private-only' will never egress. For non-sensitive routes you could enable a region-hosted fallback but that requires contractual controls and data-processing agreements.

[04:49] Sandra: We'll likely do mixed — critical clinical inference stays on-prem, analytics or non-PII workloads could go to hosted. Need a clear labeling and enforcement policy.

[04:59] Leo: We can support route-level policies enforced by the local router. Also support for audit logs that show which route was used per request.

[05:08] Alex: On updates, walk us through a typical patch flow for airgapped nodes — from Redwood releasing a patch to us applying it.

[05:15] Leo: Sure — step one: Redwood builds and signs the release artifact and publishes a release manifest. Step two: we deliver the signed bundle to you (S3 signed link for secured transfer, or we prepare an offline bundle). Step three: your operator verifies the signature with our public key, runs a pre-check script, applies in a canary node, runs smoke tests, and then stages to the rest. We provide rollback manifests if needed.

[05:39] Dr. Priya: Do we get test vectors and smoke test scripts? Our validation team will want deterministic tests.

[05:44] Leo: Yes, we provide a test-suite with deterministic seed inputs and golden outputs (where feasible) and a smoke harness that validates model outputs didn't regress beyond a threshold. The smoke harness can run locally.

[05:57] Maya: Important to call out timing windows — Alex, you mentioned maintenance windows. What times do you prefer?

[06:02] Alex: We have a weekly maintenance window Sunday 02:00–06:00 local. Critical patches only outside business hours. We may do canaries outside that window with explicit approval.

[06:12] Sandra: For compliance, we will need to see the code-signing chain and proof that release artifacts were built in a controlled CI. Also request SCA scanning reports.

[06:21] Maya: We'll share a redacted CI provenance doc and SCA summary. Some customers ask for full build logs under NDA; we can discuss that in the enterprise contract.

[06:34] Dr. Priya: Anything about telemetry? We are super strict — no outbound telemetry without our approval.

[06:40] Leo: Telemetry is opt-in. For private airgapped installs it's disabled by default. If you enable it, it's over an outbound proxy you control and we provide filters for which metrics leave.

[06:51] Alex: Let's talk performance — for the 200ms p99 requirement on some routes, do you have benchmarks for H100 vs A100 on Redwood runtime?

[07:00] Leo: We do. Generally H100 with the optimized kernels hits lower latency for medium-length sequences — but it's model dependent. We'll share model-specific pro leans — Redwood's benchmark sheets. Note that tokenization and model architecture (decoder-only vs encoder-decoder) changes latency profiles.

[07:18] Dr. Priya: We'll send 3 models and sample prompts. Could you run local-ish benchmarks or give us guidance for expected p99 on our hardware?

[07:26] Leo: Yes — best approach: share model weights or model specs and a representative prompt set, we generate a sizing recommendation and expected p99 numbers. For airgapped, we can do an offline benchmark artifact you run locally.

[07:39] Maya: Action item: Leo will produce a compatibility and sizing doc with recommended node sizes for 50–100 qps and expected p99 ranges.

[07:48] Leo: Yep, I'll include driver and CUDA matrix.

[07:53] Alex: Regarding storage — we have a central NFS for model artifacts and an NVMe pool for local caching. Any recommendations?

[08:01] Leo: Use NVMe for local cache to avoid NFS latency. Keep model artifacts on NFS or an on-prem object store; the node pulls into local NVMe cache on deploy. We recommend isolating local caches per node with quotas to avoid saturation.

[08:16] Dr. Priya: About RBAC — can we integrate with our SAML provider and map groups to roles? Also need MFA enforced for operators.

[08:25] Maya: Yes, SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning are supported; you can map groups to RBAC roles, and we support MFA through your IdP.

[08:33] Sandra: We need audit logs to be immutable and exportable to our SIEM. How do you handle log retention and tamper evidence on the node?

[08:41] Leo: We write logs to an append-only store and maintain SHA256 chain links for tamper evidence. Logs are exported as signed bundles for ingestion into SIEM. We can also configure forwarding via your SIEM proxy if you permit an outbound channel.

[08:58] Dr. Priya: What about model dropout and graceful degradation? If a node loses GPU, what's the app-visible behavior?

[09:06] Leo: The runtime will fail fast for GPU-only routes. You can configure policy-level fallbacks to CPU or to an alternative model variant with lower quality. However for health-sensitive routes you can mark them 'no-fallback' so requests fail with an explicit error and trigger an alert.

[09:23] Alex: Ok. We're also looking at deployment cadence — monthly patch cycles vs emergency patches. How fast can you deliver an emergency hotfix artifact?

[09:31] Maya: We can push hotfixes and provide emergency signed bundles within 24–48 hours depending on the severity and agreement. For emergencies we agree a fast path under an enterprise contract.

[09:42] Sandra: We'll want SLA terms in writing for response times for critical incidents.

[09:48] Maya: Absolutely — those are typically part of Dedicated/Private enterprise SOWs.

[09:54] Dr. Priya: Cost is another factor. If we go private, what's the rough shape of monthly run cost versus hosted? We know privately you have infra + license.

[10:03] Maya: Cost depends a lot on scale and the model quantization. For private we do a platform license + support + recommended reserved capacity for throughput. We'll put together a TCO model comparing hosted per-token costs vs private fixed OPEX + license amortization.

[10:18] Alex: Any restrictions on firmware updates on the GPU side? Our security team wants to keep firmware tightly controlled.

[10:24] Leo: We don't touch firmware; firmware updates are customer-controlled. Our compatibility matrix will note minimum firmware version requirements, but you apply them.

[10:33] Dr. Priya: About validation and regressions — smoke tests are fine, but for clinical models we have quality gates and human-in-the-loop checks. Can the rollout be paused until a human signs off?

[10:43] Leo: Yes. The controller supports manual gating. You can configure automated canaries, but require manual sign-off for production rollouts. We also surface detailed diffs and output drift metrics in the console (or as exported reports for airgapped installs).

[10:58] Alex: For the pilot, what do you need from us to get started?

[11:03] Maya: Typically: 1) hardware inventory and maintenance windows, 2) representative prompts and sample models, 3) compliance contacts and required artifacts, and 4) decision on whether you want telemetry/telemetry proxy.

[11:16] Dr. Priya: We'll provide those. We'll also want an NDA addendum for build logs if needed.

[11:22] Maya: Noted. We'll email a proposed NDA addendum template and the checklist.

[11:28] Sandra: One last thing — backups and disaster recovery. If the entire cluster fails, what's the restore story?

[11:35] Leo: We provide backup/export tools for model artifacts and config. You'd store encrypted backups externally (tape, S3 on air-gapped transfer). Restore is manual for sealed sites; we provide a step-by-step recovery playbook.

[11:49] Dr. Priya: Good. That helps.

[11:52] Maya: Ok, quick recap and next steps: we'll send the secure-deployment checklist, SOC2/ISO artefacts (redacted), KMS/HSM integration notes; Leo will produce a compatibility matrix and sizing doc; Alex will share hardware inventory and maintenance windows; Sandra will share compliance contacts. We'll also schedule a hardware sizing call next week. Anything to add?

[12:18] Alex: No, that covers it.

[12:22] Sandra: Nope. Thanks everyone.

[12:25] Maya: Great, we'll follow up with notes and the docs. Thanks!

[12:30] -- End of recorded portion --
